title: Evolutionary stability of environmentally induced morphological dimorphism in spatially heterogeneous systems
content:
Abstract
Phenotypic diversification without genetic divergence is a key paradox in evolutionary biology. We develop a mathematical model of two vole morphs (genus Arvicola; large aquatic and small fossorial–terrestrial) that coexist within a single genetically homogeneous population but occupy distinct ecological niches. Using a reaction–diffusion framework with environmentally driven phenotypic switching, we show that stable dimorphism can emerge in spatially and temporally heterogeneous conditions. Our analysis demonstrates that adaptive phenotypic plasticity can maintain this polymorphism across broad parameter ranges, including varying dispersal and switching regimens. Local environmental cues determine morph expression, while interactions between switching and dispersal generate spatial structure and can lead to asymmetric range expansion. We also show that this system represents an evolutionarily stable strategy that enables efficient resource use across heterogeneous landscapes, contrasting with generalist species relying on behavioural flexibility. Overall, the model shows that phenotypic plasticity alone can sustain ecological specialization without genetic divergence and provides general predictions for systems exhibiting cryptic ecological differentiation. Similar mechanisms might underlie phenotypic differentiation in other systems, including social insects and eusocial mammals, such as Heterocephalus glaber, where environmentally induced developmental pathways generate discrete morphs within structured populations.
